english.note: This is the all-purpose noun for trouble or inconvenience, including saying that something is no bother.
This is the all-purpose choice for an annoying inconvenience or a troublesome incident.
This is the all-purpose choice for an inconvenience or a troublesome thing; an annoying person is more specifically a 麻煩友.
Use this as the all-purpose choice for an unwelcome bother, demand, or presence.
Use this when the hindrance is framed as trouble or inconvenience caused to someone, rather than as a physical or abstract obstacle.
Use this when “grief” means trouble or annoyance caused by a person or situation.
This is the all-purpose everyday choice for a nuisance, annoyance, or troublesome act or thing.
Use this for trouble or inconvenience, especially when the problem is causing practical hassle.
Use this colloquial all-purpose choice for something that is a nuisance or causes annoyance.
Use this for an unpleasant nuisance or problem that causes trouble.
Use this for a troublesome matter that causes irritation rather than for the feeling itself.
Use this for a colloquial hassle or trouble that makes achieving something more difficult.
Use 麻煩 for the nuisance or troublesome-person sense of “a trial,” rather than for a religious or literary ordeal.

boxes.meaning: being in trouble, a difficult spot

english.note: Use 麻煩 for the figurative sense of being in trouble or a difficult situation.
Use this for being in a difficult situation or for extra inconvenience; in a legal context it can mean being in trouble with the authorities without naming the legal issue.
Use this colloquially when the predicament is described as trouble or an immediate problem.
Use this for being in trouble or having a difficult situation to deal with.
